definition:
The doctrine of mission concerns God's purpose to make himself known to every nation and to gather a people from all of them, and the part his people play in that purpose. The Bible begins with all humanity made in God's image and ends with “a multitude too large to count, from every nation and tribe and people and tongue” before God's throne (Revelation 7:9). Between those two pages God chooses Abraham so that “all the families of the earth will be blessed through you” (Genesis 12:3), calls Israel to live before the nations as his priestly people, promises through the prophets that his servant will be “a light for the nations” (Isaiah 49:6), and, in the risen Jesus, sends his disciples to “make disciples of all nations” (Matthew 28:19). Christians agree that the church is sent into the world to bear witness to Christ in word and deed, to call people to repentance and faith, to baptize and teach, and to plant churches among every people. They differ in how they relate proclamation of the gospel to works of mercy and justice, and in how they understand the wider ‘mission of God’ in the world.

The English word ‘mission’ comes from the Latin missio, ‘a sending’, from mittere, ‘to send’. For most of the church's history theologians used it of the Father's sending of the Son and the Spirit; its common use for sending preachers to other lands dates from the sixteenth century, when the Jesuits and other Catholic orders adopted it. The biblical vocabulary is richer. The Hebrew shalach, ‘send’, is used of God sending prophets (Isaiah 6:8) and of Jonah's commission to Nineveh. The Greek verbs apostellō and pempō both mean ‘send’; John uses them interchangeably, and Jesus uses both in one sentence: “As the Father has sent Me, so also I am sending you” (John 20:21). From apostellō comes apostolos, ‘one who is sent’, an envoy. The Hebrew goyim and the Greek ethnē mean ‘nations’ or ‘peoples’, and in the plural they often mean ‘the Gentiles’, the non-Jewish peoples. The New Testament also speaks of martys, a ‘witness’ who testifies to what he has seen (Acts 1:8); only later, because so many witnesses died for their testimony, did the word come to mean ‘martyr’. And euangelizomai means ‘announce good news’, the root of ‘evangelism’.
ot:
Mission begins with creation. God blesses the first humans and tells them to “fill the earth” (Genesis 1:28), a command repeated to Noah (Genesis 9:1), and Genesis 10 traces how “the nations of the earth spread out after the flood” (Genesis 10:32), each with its own lands and languages. At Babel humanity refuses to scatter and tries to “make a name for ourselves” (Genesis 11:4). The next chapter answers Babel. God promises Abram, “I will make your name great,” and his purpose reaches past Abram's family: “all the families of the earth will be blessed through you” (Genesis 12:2-3). The promise is repeated to Abraham (Genesis 18:18; 22:18), to Isaac (Genesis 26:4), and to Jacob (Genesis 28:14), and God renames Abram “a father of many nations” (Genesis 17:5). Paul later calls this promise the gospel announced in advance (Galatians 3:8). From its first chapter, then, the story of God's chosen people is a story told for the sake of the world.

Israel's calling carries the same outward face. When the Israelites leave Egypt, “a mixed multitude also went up with them” (Exodus 12:38), and God's acts against Pharaoh are so that “My name might be proclaimed in all the earth” (Exodus 9:16). At Sinai the whole earth is God's, and Israel is to be “a kingdom of priests” (Exodus 19:5-6), standing between God and the nations as priests stand between God and the people. Outsiders are woven into Israel's story: Rahab of Jericho, Ruth the Moabite, whose confession is “your people will be my people, and your God will be my God” (Ruth 1:16), the widow of Zarephath, and Naaman the Syrian commander, who declared, “there is no God in all the earth except in Israel” (2 Kings 5:15). At the dedication of the temple Solomon prays for “the foreigner who is not of Your people Israel” who comes to pray there, “Then all the peoples of the earth will know Your name and fear You” (1 Kings 8:41-43). The Psalms call on the nations again and again: “Declare His glory among the nations” (Psalm 96:3), and “Praise the LORD, all you nations” (Psalm 117:1). Psalm 67 asks God to bless Israel “that Your ways may be known on earth, Your salvation among all nations” (Psalm 67:2). Scholars such as Johannes Blauw (The Missionary Nature of the Church, 1962) have described Israel's role as chiefly ‘centripetal’: the nations are drawn in to Israel's God, rather than Israel being sent out to them.

The prophets widen the vision. Isaiah and Micah both foresee the day when “all nations will stream” to the mountain of the LORD's house to learn his ways (Isaiah 2:2-3; Micah 4:1-2). Isaiah's servant is appointed “to be a covenant for the people and a light to the nations” (Isaiah 42:6), and God tells him that restoring Israel alone is too small a thing: “I will also make You a light for the nations, to bring My salvation to the ends of the earth” (Isaiah 49:6). God calls, “Turn to Me and be saved, all the ends of the earth” (Isaiah 45:22), promises that his house “will be called a house of prayer for all the nations” (Isaiah 56:7), and even names Israel's old enemies as his own: “Blessed be Egypt My people, Assyria My handiwork, and Israel My inheritance” (Isaiah 19:25). Isaiah's last chapter pictures God gathering “all nations and tongues” and sending survivors to distant peoples who “have not heard of My fame” (Isaiah 66:18-19), the nearest the Old Testament comes to an outward sending. The book of Jonah is a sharp exception and a rebuke: God sends a reluctant prophet to Israel's enemy Nineveh, spares the city when it repents, and ends by asking whether he should not care about its people (Jonah 4:11). Daniel sees one like a son of man given a kingdom so “that the people of every nation and language should serve Him” (Daniel 7:14), and Malachi declares that God's name “will be great among the nations” (Malachi 1:11).
nt:
The New Testament opens with the nations already present. Matthew's genealogy of Jesus names Rahab and Ruth (Matthew 1:5), and Magi from the east come to worship the newborn king (Matthew 2:1-2). Simeon greets the infant as “a light for revelation to the Gentiles” (Luke 2:32), echoing Isaiah. Jesus' own ministry was directed mainly to Israel; he told the Twelve, “Go rather to the lost sheep of Israel” (Matthew 10:6), and said, “I was sent only to the lost sheep of the house of Israel” (Matthew 15:24). Yet he healed a centurion's servant and a Canaanite woman's daughter, spoke of “many” who “will come from the east and the west to share the banquet with Abraham” (Matthew 8:11), and in Nazareth recalled that Elijah and Elisha had been sent to a Sidonian widow and a Syrian leper (Luke 4:25-27). When he cleared the temple he quoted Isaiah: “My house will be called a house of prayer for all the nations” (Mark 11:17). The order is from Israel to the nations, not Israel instead of the nations. He also taught that “the gospel must first be proclaimed to all the nations” (Mark 13:10) before the end.

After the resurrection each Gospel and Acts gives a form of Jesus' commission. In Matthew the risen Jesus, to whom “All authority in heaven and on earth has been given,” says, “Therefore go and make disciples of all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit, and teaching them to obey all that I have commanded you,” with the promise “surely I am with you always, even to the end of the age” (Matthew 28:18-20). The main verb is the imperative ‘make disciples’; ‘go’ is a participle, but in this construction it shares the force of the command, so the common claim that Jesus only meant ‘as you are going’ does not hold up grammatically. ‘Baptizing’ and ‘teaching’ describe how disciples are made. Whether panta ta ethnē, ‘all the nations’, refers to ethnic peoples as groups or simply to all people, Gentiles included, is debated: Ralph Winter and Donald McGavran stressed people groups, while other scholars read the phrase more generally. In Luke, repentance and forgiveness “will be proclaimed to all nations, beginning in Jerusalem,” and the disciples are “witnesses” (Luke 24:47-48). In John, the Son's own sending is the pattern for theirs (John 20:21; 17:18). And in Acts Jesus promises, “you will receive power when the Holy Spirit comes upon you, and you will be My witnesses in Jerusalem, and in all Judea and Samaria, and to the ends of the earth” (Acts 1:8), a sentence that also outlines the book.

Acts tells how the church moved outward, often pushed rather than planned. Pentecost gathers Jews “from every nation under heaven” (Acts 2:5), a reversal of Babel in which each hears in his own language. Persecution scatters believers who “preached the word wherever they went” (Acts 8:4); Philip preaches in Samaria and baptizes an Ethiopian official; Peter learns at Cornelius's house that “God does not show favoritism, but welcomes those from every nation who fear Him” (Acts 10:34-35); unnamed believers from Cyprus and Cyrene begin speaking to Greeks in Antioch (Acts 11:20). The church at Antioch, led by the Spirit, sets apart Barnabas and Saul and sends them off with prayer and the laying on of hands (Acts 13:2-3), and Paul and Barnabas apply Isaiah's servant text to their own work: “I have made you a light for the Gentiles” (Acts 13:47). James at the Jerusalem council reads the Gentile mission as God taking “from them a people to be His own” (Acts 15:14), in fulfillment of Amos. The book ends with Paul in Rome proclaiming the kingdom “Boldly and freely” (Acts 28:31).

Paul understood his calling as an apostle to the Gentiles, sent “to call all those among the Gentiles to the obedience that comes from faith” (Romans 1:5), and he made it his ambition “to preach the gospel where Christ was not known” (Romans 15:20). His strategy was to preach, gather converts into churches, appoint elders, and move on, while churches like Philippi shared in his work through “partnership in the gospel” (Philippians 1:5). He argued that calling on the Lord requires hearing, and hearing requires preachers who are sent (Romans 10:14-15). He called believers “ambassadors for Christ” entrusted with “the message of reconciliation” (2 Corinthians 5:19-20), and adapted himself to every culture he entered: “I have become all things to all people so that by all possible means I might save some” (1 Corinthians 9:22). Peter tells scattered believers that their good conduct among the Gentiles is itself a witness (1 Peter 2:12). The mystery Paul proclaims is that “the Gentiles are fellow heirs, fellow members of the body, and fellow partakers of the promise in Christ Jesus” (Ephesians 3:6), and he looks to the day when “every tongue” will “confess that Jesus Christ is Lord” (Philippians 2:11). Revelation shows the goal. The Lamb has purchased people “from every tribe and tongue and people and nation” (Revelation 5:9), and in the new Jerusalem “the glory and honor of the nations” is brought into the city (Revelation 21:26) and the leaves of the tree of life are “for the healing of the nations” (Revelation 22:2).

keyTexts.why: God's call of Abram answers Babel: through one family all the families of the earth will be blessed. Paul calls this promise the gospel announced in advance (Galatians 3:8).
Israel is God's treasured possession because the whole earth is his, and it is to be a kingdom of priests, God's people placed among the nations.
Solomon prays that foreigners who come to the temple will be heard, so that all the peoples of the earth will know God's name.
Israel asks for God's blessing so that his salvation will be known among all nations and all peoples will praise him.
The servant will be a light for the nations, bringing God's salvation to the ends of the earth. Paul and Barnabas apply it to their mission (Acts 13:47).
God rebukes his prophet's anger at the sparing of Nineveh and asks whether he should not care for its people. The Old Testament's sharpest lesson in God's compassion for the nations.
The risen Christ, holding all authority, commands his disciples to make disciples of all nations, baptizing and teaching them, and promises his presence to the end of the age.
Christ's suffering and resurrection and the proclamation of repentance and forgiveness to all nations are together what the Scriptures foretold.
As the Father sent the Son, the Son sends his disciples, and he breathes the Holy Spirit on them. The church's sending is patterned on Christ's.
The Spirit empowers the disciples to be witnesses from Jerusalem to the ends of the earth, the program of the book of Acts.
The church at Antioch, at the Spirit's word, sets apart Barnabas and Saul and sends them out, the first planned mission beyond Syria and Judea.
Calling on the Lord requires believing, believing requires hearing, and hearing requires preachers who are sent.
God has reconciled the world to himself in Christ and entrusted his people with the message of reconciliation as his ambassadors.
The mystery now revealed is that Gentiles are fellow heirs and members of one body, and the church displays God's wisdom to the powers.
A countless multitude from every nation, tribe, people, and language stands before the throne and the Lamb. The end toward which mission moves.

history:
The first Christian centuries saw the faith spread chiefly through ordinary believers, traders, and families, as well as through preachers, across the Roman Empire and beyond it into Mesopotamia, Persia, Armenia, Ethiopia, and India. Ulfilas translated the Bible into Gothic in the fourth century, setting a pattern of translation into the languages of new peoples that the church has followed ever since. Patrick preached in Ireland in the fifth century; Columba founded the monastery of Iona off Scotland in 563; Pope Gregory the Great sent Augustine to the kingdom of Kent in 597; Boniface worked among the Germanic peoples in the eighth century; and Cyril and Methodius went to Moravia in 863, creating an alphabet for the Slavic language so that the Scriptures and liturgy could be heard in it. In the East, the Church of the East carried the gospel along the trade routes of Asia: the Xi'an Stele, set up in 781, records the arrival of the monk Alopen in the Chinese capital in 635. These centuries also brought grave distortions, such as Charlemagne's wars against the Saxons in the late eighth century, in which baptism was imposed by force.

From the sixteenth century, Catholic orders carried the faith to the Americas, Africa, and Asia alongside Spanish and Portuguese empires. Francis Xavier reached India in 1542 and Japan in 1549, and Matteo Ricci lived and taught in China until his death in Beijing in 1610, seeking to express the faith in terms Chinese scholars could understand. Bartolomé de las Casas protested the enslavement and killing of the native peoples of the Americas, arguing at Valladolid (1550 to 1551) against those who justified it. The Protestant churches were slower to send missionaries abroad; in 1651 the theological faculty of Wittenberg gave the opinion that the command of Matthew 28 had been fulfilled by the apostles, and Justinian von Welz's appeals in the 1660s for Lutheran missions were rebuffed. Pietism changed this: Danish-Halle missionaries went to Tranquebar in India in 1706, and in 1732 the Moravian community at Herrnhut sent Leonard Dober and David Nitschmann to enslaved Africans on St. Thomas in the Caribbean. William Carey's An Enquiry into the Obligations of Christians to Use Means for the Conversion of the Heathens (1792) argued that the commission binds the church in every age, and he sailed for India in 1793 with the new Baptist Missionary Society. The nineteenth century became the great age of Protestant missionary societies, including Hudson Taylor's China Inland Mission (1865). Henry Venn of the Church Missionary Society and Rufus Anderson of the American Board urged that mission churches become self-governing, self-supporting, and self-propagating, and Roland Allen's Missionary Methods: St. Paul's or Ours? (1912) pressed the same point from Paul's practice.

The World Missionary Conference at Edinburgh in 1910, chaired by John R. Mott, is often taken as the starting point of the modern ecumenical movement. In the decades after, Karl Barth's address at the Brandenburg missionary conference (1932) and the International Missionary Council's meeting at Willingen (1952) shaped the idea that mission belongs first to God and that the church participates in it; Karl Hartenstein used the Latin phrase missio Dei in his report on Willingen, and it became a byword of twentieth-century mission theology. The Second Vatican Council's decree Ad Gentes (1965) taught that the pilgrim church is missionary by its very nature, a theme continued in Paul VI's Evangelii Nuntiandi (1975) and John Paul II's Redemptoris Missio (1990). Among evangelicals, the International Congress on World Evangelization at Lausanne (1974) produced the Lausanne Covenant, largely drafted by John Stott, which affirmed both evangelism and social responsibility as Christian duty while stating that evangelism is primary in the church's mission; Latin American theologians such as René Padilla and Samuel Escobar pressed at the same congress for what they called integral mission. Later scholarship, including David Bosch's Transforming Mission (1991), Lesslie Newbigin's writings on the gospel in Western culture, and Lamin Sanneh's Translating the Message (1989), which argued that translation into local languages has allowed peoples to receive the faith on their own terms, reshaped the field. By the late twentieth century most of the world's Christians lived in Africa, Asia, and Latin America, and churches there now send missionaries of their own around the world.

differ.view: Evangelism as the church's primary task
differ.body: The church's distinctive mission is to proclaim the gospel of Christ crucified and risen, call people to repentance and faith, baptize them, gather them into churches, and teach them to obey Christ (Matthew 28:18-20). Christians should do good to all people and seek justice as their neighbors and citizens, and churches do works of mercy, but these flow from and serve the proclamation of the gospel rather than standing alongside it as equal parts of one mission. The Lausanne Covenant (1974) states that in the church's mission of sacrificial service, evangelism is primary, and the Lausanne consultation at Grand Rapids (1982) spoke of its logical priority. Defenders argue that only the church can preach the gospel, that eternal matters outweigh temporal ones, and that when mission means everything the church does, proclamation tends to be crowded out. Writers such as Kevin DeYoung and Greg Gilbert (What Is the Mission of the Church?, 2011) take this view.

The gospel is the good news of God's kingdom, and the church's mission is to embody and proclaim it in every part of life. Jesus preached, healed, fed, and welcomed the outcast, and announced good news to the poor (Luke 4:18-19), and the prophets and apostles joined faith with justice (James 2:14-17). Evangelism and social action are not two tasks to be ranked but two sides of one witness: proclamation has social consequences, social involvement bears witness to Christ, and to separate them distorts both. This view was pressed at Lausanne in 1974 by Latin American theologians René Padilla and Samuel Escobar and was expressed in the Micah Network's Declaration on Integral Mission (2001). Defenders argue that a message about Christ's love that ignores the hungry and oppressed contradicts itself, and that deeds of mercy and justice make the spoken gospel credible.

differ.view: Missio Dei in the ecumenical tradition
differ.body: Mission belongs first to God: the Father sends the Son, the Father and the Son send the Spirit, and the triune God sends the church into the world. God is at work in the whole of history, reconciling, liberating, and renewing, and the church's task is to discern and join that work rather than to own mission as its own program. In this tradition, shaped by the International Missionary Council and the World Council of Churches after Willingen (1952), mission includes evangelism but also dialogue, the pursuit of peace and justice, and care for creation, and it is carried out in humility and in partnership with churches in every land. Defenders, including many who follow David Bosch's synthesis, argue that this view is grounded in the Trinity, corrects the colonial legacy of mission, and recognizes that the church is the servant of God's mission and not its master.

Catholic teaching since Ad Gentes (1965) holds that the church is missionary by its nature, because it originates in the sending of the Son and the Spirit. Evangelization includes proclaiming Christ, planting the church where it does not yet exist, and inculturation, the expression of the faith in the forms of each culture, together with works of charity and human development; Paul VI's Evangelii Nuntiandi (1975) insisted there is no true evangelization without the explicit proclamation of Jesus. The Orthodox churches emphasize that the Eucharistic liturgy is itself the heart of witness and that its life should overflow into the world, an idea the Romanian theologian Ion Bria called the ‘liturgy after the liturgy’, and they point to the historic Orthodox practice, from Cyril and Methodius onward, of translating Scripture and worship into local languages and raising up local clergy.

errors:
The church has repeatedly had to reject the confusion of mission with conquest. When the gospel was carried by armies or imposed by rulers, as in Charlemagne's forced baptisms of the Saxons or in the conquests of the Americas, it was contradicted by the very means used to spread it. Jesus rejected the sword (Matthew 26:52), sent his disciples as sheep among wolves, and told Pilate his kingdom was not of this world. A related error equates the gospel with the culture of the missionary, so that converts must adopt a foreign language, dress, or politics to follow Christ. The Jerusalem council's refusal to require Gentiles to become Jews (Acts 15) is the church's first ruling against that error, and Paul's practice of becoming “all things to all people” (1 Corinthians 9:22) sets the pattern. Many churches have acknowledged and repented of the ways their missions served colonial power and racial prejudice, while also honoring missionaries who opposed those abuses.

An opposite error treats mission as optional, the concern of a few specialists, or as finished. The Wittenberg faculty's opinion of 1651 is one example, and every church that settles into caring only for its own members repeats it. The New Testament treats witness as the calling of the whole church (1 Peter 2:9; Acts 8:4). Other distortions include reducing mission to social improvement with no call to faith in Christ, reducing it to counting decisions with no concern for making disciples who obey all Christ commanded, and motivating it by guilt or by the missionary's own heroism rather than by the love of God and the glory of Christ. Finally, some have claimed that God's saving purpose for the nations cancels his faithfulness to Israel, a claim Paul rejects when he says that God's gifts and calling are irrevocable and that Gentile inclusion and Israel's future belong together (Romans 11:25-29).
life:
The doctrine of mission tells Christians that their faith was never meant to stop with them. Every believer received the gospel because someone crossed a boundary to bring it, and every believer is now part of the people through whom God intends to bless the families of the earth. For most Christians, mission happens first where they already live: in the way they work, treat neighbors, show hospitality, speak of Christ when there is occasion, and care for the poor. Peter's instruction to live honorably among unbelievers so that they may see good deeds and glorify God (1 Peter 2:12) applies to office, classroom, and street. It also calls for prayer, since Jesus told his disciples to “Ask the Lord of the harvest” to send out workers (Matthew 9:38), and for generosity, since Paul's churches shared in the work by supporting those who went.

The doctrine also shapes how Christians see the world and themselves. Because God's purpose embraces every nation, no people is beneath his concern and no culture is the owner of the gospel. Christians in any one land belong to a worldwide body that is now mostly non-Western, and they have much to receive from believers elsewhere as well as much to give. And mission gives hope. The same Lord who commanded his disciples to go promised to be with them always, and the Bible's last vision is not of a shrinking remnant but of a multitude from every tribe and language worshiping the Lamb. That end is certain, and it frees believers to bear witness with patience, humility, and confidence rather than anxiety.
questions: Genesis 12 follows directly after Babel. How does reading God's promise to Abram against the scattering of the nations in Genesis 10 and 11 shape your understanding of what mission is for?

Jesus sent his disciples first to Israel and then to all nations. What do the Great Commission texts in Matthew 28, Luke 24, John 20, and Acts 1 each add to the picture, and what would be lost if we read only one of them?
Christians differ on how evangelism relates to works of mercy and justice. What do the positions described here agree on, and how might a local church hold both together in practice?
